prompt: Which statement describes the particles in a **solid**?

options.text: Close together in a regular pattern, vibrating in fixed positions
Close together but able to slide past each other
Far apart and moving quickly in all directions
Close together in a regular pattern and not moving at all

feedback.b: That describes a liquid. Its particles can slide past each other, which is why liquids flow.
feedback.d: Particles in a solid are always moving. They vibrate on the spot, even though they can't leave their positions.

hints: Think about why a solid keeps its shape.
Particles are always moving, even in a solid.
solution: In a solid the particles are packed closely in a regular pattern. Strong forces hold them in fixed positions, but they still **vibrate** on the spot.

prompt: What is the name of the change of state from a **gas** to a **liquid**?
hints: It's what happens when water vapour hits a cold window.
It is the opposite of evaporation.
solution: **Condensation.** The gas particles lose energy, slow down and are pulled together to form a liquid, such as droplets on a cold window.

prompt: Match each change of state to what happens.
hints: Sublimation skips the liquid state.
solution: Melting: solid → liquid. Freezing: liquid → solid. Evaporation: liquid → gas. Condensation: gas → liquid. Sublimation: solid → gas, with no liquid in between.

prompt: A liquid has a fixed [[a]], but it takes the [[b]] of its container.
hints: Pour 250 mL of water from a jug into a glass. What stays the same, and what changes?
solution: A liquid has a fixed **volume** (250 mL stays 250 mL), but it takes the **shape** of whatever container it is in, because its particles can slide past each other.

prompt: What happens to the particles in a substance when it is heated?

options.text: They move faster
They get bigger
They start to melt
They get heavier

feedback.b: The particles stay the same size. They move faster and spread further apart, so the substance takes up more space.
feedback.c: A substance can melt, but a single particle doesn't melt. Melting is about how particles are arranged.
feedback.d: The particles' mass doesn't change when they are heated.

hints: Heating gives the particles more energy.
solution: Heating gives particles more energy, so they **move faster** (vibrate faster in a solid). The particles themselves don't change size or mass.

figure.alt: Three boxes of particles. Box A: a few particles spread far apart. Box B: particles packed tightly in neat rows and columns. Box C: particles close together and touching, but jumbled, in the lower part of the box.

options.text: Box A
Box B
Box C

feedback.a: Particles that are far apart are a gas.
feedback.b: Particles in a neat, regular pattern are a solid.

hints: Liquid particles are close together, like a solid's, but not arranged in a pattern.
solution: **Box C.** The particles are close together but jumbled, so they can slide past each other. Box A is a gas (far apart) and Box B is a solid (regular pattern).

prompt: Why can a gas be squashed (compressed) much more easily than a liquid?

options.text: There is a lot of empty space between gas particles
Gas particles are much smaller than liquid particles
Gas particles can be squashed into a smaller size
Gas particles are not moving

feedback.b: Water vapour and liquid water are made of the same particles. The difference is the space between them.
feedback.c: Particles can't be squashed smaller. Compressing a gas pushes the particles closer together.
feedback.d: Gas particles move very fast, faster than in a liquid or solid.

hints: Think about how far apart the particles are in each state.
solution: Gas particles are far apart with lots of **empty space** between them, so pushing on a gas moves the particles closer together. In a liquid the particles are already touching, so there's almost no space to squash.

prompt: Which of these is an example of **sublimation**?

options.text: Dry ice (solid carbon dioxide) turning straight into a gas
An ice cube melting in a drink
Water boiling in a jug
Water droplets forming on a cold can of drink

feedback.b: That is melting: solid → liquid.

hints: Sublimation goes from solid to gas without becoming a liquid first.
solution: Sublimation is solid → gas without melting first. **Dry ice** does this at about −78 °C, which is why it never leaves a puddle. (The white 'smoke' around it is tiny droplets of water from the air, condensed by the very cold gas. Carbon dioxide gas itself is invisible.)

prompt: In which of these changes do the particles **gain** energy? Select **all** that apply.

options.text: Melting
Freezing
Boiling
Condensation
Sublimation

hints: Particles gain energy when a substance is heated.
Which changes go towards a state where the particles move more freely?
solution: **Melting, boiling and sublimation** all need heat: the particles gain energy and move more freely (solid → liquid, liquid → gas, solid → gas). In freezing and condensation the particles lose energy.

prompt: What is the name of the process where particles spread out from where there are lots of them to where there are fewer, because of their random movement?
hints: It's how a smell spreads across a room.
The word starts with d.
solution: **Diffusion.** Particles move randomly, so over time they spread from an area of high concentration to an area of low concentration.

prompt: Evaporation happens only at the [[a]] of a liquid, and it can happen at [[b]] temperature. Boiling happens [[c]] the liquid, at the boiling point.
hints: A puddle dries up on a mild day without ever reaching 100 °C.
When water boils, where do the bubbles form?
solution: Evaporation happens at the **surface**, at **any** temperature: only the particles near the top can escape. Boiling happens **throughout** the liquid, with bubbles of gas forming inside it, at the boiling point.

prompt: A drop of food colouring is gently added to three beakers of still water at different temperatures. Put the beakers in order, from the one where the colour spreads **fastest** to the one where it spreads **slowest**.
hints: How does temperature affect the speed of particles?
solution: At a higher temperature the particles have more energy and move faster, so diffusion is fastest at **60 °C**, then 30 °C, and slowest at 10 °C.

prompt: A block of ice at −10 °C is heated steadily until it becomes steam at 110 °C. Put the stages in order.

items.text: The liquid water warms up to 100 °C

hints: Ice melts at 0 °C and water boils at 100 °C.
The temperature stays the same while the state is changing.
solution: The ice warms to 0 °C → melts at 0 °C → the water warms to 100 °C → boils at 100 °C → the steam warms above 100 °C. During melting and boiling the temperature stays steady, because the energy is being used to overcome the forces between the particles.

stem: Substance X has a melting point of −20 °C and a boiling point of 60 °C.
prompt: At room temperature (20 °C), substance X is a [[a]].
hints: Is 20 °C below the melting point, between the two, or above the boiling point?
solution: 20 °C is above the melting point (−20 °C), so X has melted, but below the boiling point (60 °C), so it hasn't boiled. X is a **liquid**.

stem: Substance X has a melting point of −20 °C and a boiling point of 60 °C.
prompt: Gaseous X at 90 °C is cooled slowly. At what temperature will it start to condense into a liquid?
hints: Condensation is the reverse of boiling.
solution: Condensation is the reverse of boiling, so it happens at the same temperature as the boiling point: **60 °C**.

prompt: A puddle dries up on a sunny day, even though the water never gets anywhere near 100 °C. Why?

options.text: Some particles at the surface have enough energy to escape as a gas
Sunlight makes water boil at a much lower temperature
The water particles break down into hydrogen and oxygen
The water particles shrink until they can't be seen

feedback.b: The water isn't boiling. There are no bubbles forming inside it. This is evaporation.
feedback.c: That would be a chemical change. Evaporation is a physical change; the water is still water, just as a gas.
feedback.d: Particles don't shrink. The water is still there in the air, as water vapour.

hints: This is evaporation, not boiling.
Not every particle has the same energy. Some move faster than others.
solution: This is **evaporation**. Particles in a liquid have a range of energies. Some fast-moving particles at the surface have enough energy to escape into the air as water vapour. Over time the whole puddle evaporates.

prompt: Use the particle model to explain why a solid has a fixed shape but a liquid does not.
modelAnswer: In a solid, strong forces of attraction hold the particles in fixed positions. They can only vibrate on the spot, so the solid keeps its shape. In a liquid, the particles are still close together, but they can move and slide past each other, so the liquid flows and takes the shape of its container.

rubric.criterion: Solid: particles are held in fixed positions by strong forces and can only vibrate
Liquid: particles can move or slide past each other, so the liquid flows and takes the shape of its container

hints: Describe how the particles can move in each state.
solution: Solid particles are locked in fixed positions, vibrating on the spot, so the shape can't change. Liquid particles can slide past each other, so a liquid flows into the shape of its container.

prompt:
A student sorts some materials into two groups.

- **Group A:** copper wire, aluminium foil, steel spoon
- **Group B:** plastic ruler, wooden pencil, rubber band

Which physical property did the student most likely use?

options.text: Whether they conduct electricity
Whether they are magnetic
Whether they float on water
Whether they are solid at room temperature

feedback.b: Copper and aluminium are not magnetic, so they wouldn't be grouped with steel this way.
feedback.c: Whether something floats depends on its density and shape, and it doesn't split these items neatly into these two groups.
feedback.d: All six materials are solids, so this property wouldn't separate them.

hints: What do all the materials in Group A have in common? (They are all metals.)
solution: Group A are all metals, which **conduct electricity**. Group B are all insulators. Copper and aluminium are not magnetic, and every item is a solid, so those properties don't explain the groups.

prompt: After a hot shower, water vapour touches a cold mirror. The water particles lose [[a]], slow down and are pulled closer together, forming droplets. This change of state is called [[b]].
hints: The mirror is colder than the vapour.
Gas → liquid has its own name.
solution: The particles lose **energy** to the cold mirror, slow down, and the forces of attraction pull them together into a liquid. Gas → liquid is **condensation**.

prompt: Which of these would make wet washing on a clothesline dry **faster**? Select **all** that apply.

options.text: A warmer day
A windy day
Spreading the clothes out
A still, humid day
Folding the clothes in a pile

hints: Drying is evaporation.
Think about particle energy, the area of the surface, and what happens to the water vapour once it has escaped.
solution: Drying is evaporation. A **warmer day** gives particles more energy, **wind** carries the water vapour away so more can escape, and **spreading the clothes out** gives a bigger surface for particles to escape from. Humid, still air and a folded pile slow it down.

prompt: Select **all** the physical properties.

options.text: Melting point
Colour
Density
Whether it conducts electricity
Whether it burns in air
Whether it reacts with acid

hints: A physical property can be observed or measured without turning the substance into something new.
Burning and reacting both make new substances.
solution: **Melting point, colour, density and electrical conductivity** are physical properties: you can measure them without making a new substance. Burning and reacting with acid make new substances, so they are chemical properties.

prompt: When ice melts, its temperature stays at 0 °C until all the ice has melted, even though heat energy is still going into it. Use the particle model to explain why.
modelAnswer: The ice is still taking in heat energy while it melts. This energy is used to overcome (break) the forces of attraction that hold the particles in their fixed positions, so the particles can start sliding past each other. Because the energy goes into changing the arrangement of the particles rather than making them move faster, the temperature doesn't rise until all of the ice has melted.

rubric.criterion: States that heat energy is still being taken in during melting
The energy is used to overcome the forces of attraction holding the particles in fixed positions
So the energy doesn't make the particles move faster, and the temperature stays the same until all the ice has melted

hints: What has to happen to the forces between particles for a solid to become a liquid?
Temperature depends on how fast the particles are moving.
solution: The heat energy goes into overcoming the forces of attraction that hold the particles in place, not into making them move faster. Temperature measures how fast particles move, so it stays at 0 °C until every particle has broken free.

prompt: 20 g of dry ice (solid carbon dioxide) is sealed inside a strong balloon. The dry ice slowly turns into carbon dioxide gas and the balloon swells up. What is the mass of the carbon dioxide inside the balloon once all the dry ice has turned into gas?
hints: The balloon is sealed, so nothing can get in or out.
A change of state doesn't create or destroy any particles.
solution: During a change of state no particles are created or destroyed, and none can escape from the sealed balloon. The particles just move much further apart, which is why the balloon swells. The mass is still **20 g**.

prompt: Sweating helps to cool you down. Why does sweat evaporating from your skin cool you?

options.text: The particles with the most energy escape, so the particles left behind have less energy on average
Sweat is colder than your skin to begin with
Evaporation gives out heat into your skin
The sweat particles take in cold from the air

feedback.b: Sweat comes out at body temperature. The cooling happens as it evaporates.
feedback.c: It's the other way round: evaporation takes energy away from your skin.
feedback.d: 'Cold' isn't something that can flow. Cooling means energy is being taken away.

hints: Which particles are able to escape from the surface of a liquid?
solution: Only the fastest, highest-energy particles escape from the surface. The particles left behind have less energy on average, so the sweat and your skin under it cool down. Energy is carried away from your body.

prompt: Diffusion happens much faster in gases than in liquids. Which is the best explanation?

options.text: Gas particles move faster and have much more space to move into
Gas particles are smaller than liquid particles
Gas particles are lighter than liquid particles of the same substance
Gas particles attract each other more strongly

feedback.b: The particles are the same size in every state. Only their spacing and movement change.
feedback.c: Steam and liquid water are made of identical water particles with the same mass.
feedback.d: It's the other way round: the forces between gas particles are very weak.

hints: Compare how fast the particles move, and how much space there is, in a gas and in a liquid.
solution: Gas particles move **faster** and have lots of **empty space**, so they spread out quickly. In a liquid, the particles are close together and keep bumping into each other, so they spread out more slowly.

prompt: A student drops a purple crystal of potassium permanganate into the bottom of a beaker of still water. An hour later the purple colour has spread through all of the water. Explain what happened, and predict how the result would change if the water were hotter.
modelAnswer: The crystal dissolves, and its particles move about randomly, colliding with the water particles. Over time the purple particles spread from where there are lots of them (around the crystal) to where there are fewer, until they are spread evenly through the water. This is diffusion. In hotter water the particles have more energy and move faster, so the colour would spread through the water more quickly.

rubric.criterion: Particles move randomly and collide with water particles
They spread from high concentration to low concentration (diffusion) until evenly spread
Hotter water: particles have more energy and move faster, so the colour spreads faster

hints: Name the process first.
How does temperature affect the movement of particles?
solution: This is diffusion: random movement spreads the purple particles from high concentration to low concentration until they are spread evenly. Hotter water means faster-moving particles, so the colour would spread more quickly.

prompt: For most substances, the solid sinks in its own liquid, because its particles are packed more closely. But ice floats on water. What does this tell you?

options.text: In ice, the water particles are held slightly further apart than in liquid water
Ice particles are lighter than liquid water particles
Ice particles aren't moving, so they weigh less
Ice is made of different particles from liquid water

feedback.b: Ice and liquid water are made of exactly the same water particles, with the same mass.
feedback.c: Ice particles do vibrate, and how much a particle moves doesn't change its mass.
feedback.d: Melting is a physical change. Ice and liquid water are both made of water particles.

hints: If the same particles take up more space, is the substance more or less dense?
solution: Ice floats because it is less dense than liquid water. The particles are the same, so they must be **spaced slightly further apart** in ice. When water freezes, its particles lock into an open pattern. Water is an unusual exception to the simple particle model, and it's why ponds freeze from the top down.

prompt: Describe how the **arrangement** and **movement** of the particles at point D are different from at point A.
modelAnswer: At A the substance is a solid. Its particles are packed closely in fixed positions in a regular pattern, and they can only vibrate. At D it is a hot liquid. The particles are still close together, but they are jumbled and not held in fixed positions, and they move around and slide past each other, faster than at A because they have more energy.

rubric.criterion: Arrangement: at A (solid) the particles are in fixed positions in a regular pattern; at D (liquid) they are still close together but jumbled, not in fixed positions
Movement: at A the particles only vibrate; at D they move around and slide past each other, and faster, because they have more energy

hints: What state is the substance in at A, and at D?
Think about both how the particles are arranged and how they move.
solution: A is a solid (fixed, regular pattern, vibrating only). D is a liquid at a higher temperature (close but jumbled, sliding past each other and moving faster).

stem: To cook a hāngī, stones are heated in a fire until they are very hot and then placed in a pit. Baskets of food go on top, covered with wet cloths or sacks, and the pit is covered with earth. Water from the wet cloths turns to steam on the hot stones, and the steam cooks the food.
prompt: When water from the wet cloths touches the hot stones, its particles [[a]] energy and move [[b]]. They spread far apart, and the water becomes steam, which is a [[c]].
hints: The stones are much hotter than the water, so heat flows into the water.
solution: The water particles **gain** energy from the hot stones, move **faster** and spread far apart. The water turns into steam, which is a **gas**.

stem: To cook a hāngī, stones are heated in a fire until they are very hot and then placed in a pit. Baskets of food go on top, covered with wet cloths or sacks, and the pit is covered with earth. Water from the wet cloths turns to steam on the hot stones, and the steam cooks the food.
prompt: When the steam reaches the cooler food, it condenses into water droplets. How does this help to cook the food?

options.text: The steam particles lose energy as they condense, and that energy heats the food
Condensing takes in heat from the food, which cooks it
The steam particles split into hydrogen and oxygen, which heat the food
The water particles get bigger as they condense and squeeze heat into the food

feedback.b: Taking heat from the food would cool it down. Condensing is the reverse of evaporating, so it gives energy out.
feedback.c: Condensing is a physical change. The water particles stay as water particles.
feedback.d: Particles never change size when they change state. Only the spaces between them change.

hints: Evaporating needs energy. What happens to that energy when the steam turns back into water?
solution: The steam particles **lose energy** as they slow down and come together into droplets. That energy is transferred to the food and heats it. Condensing gives out the energy that was taken in when the water evaporated.

stem: To cook a hāngī, stones are heated in a fire until they are very hot and then placed in a pit. Baskets of food go on top, covered with wet cloths or sacks, and the pit is covered with earth. Water from the wet cloths turns to steam on the hot stones, and the steam cooks the food.
prompt: When the hāngī is opened, people on the other side of the field soon smell the food, even though there is no wind. Use the particle model to explain why.
modelAnswer: Particles of gas carrying the smell escape from the hot food. Like air particles, they are always moving randomly in all directions and bumping into air particles. Because of this random movement they spread out from the pit, where there are lots of them, to where there are fewer, until some reach people across the field. This spreading is called diffusion.

rubric.criterion: The smell particles (gas) are always moving randomly and mix with the air particles
They spread from where there are many of them (the pit) to where there are fewer, i.e. diffusion

hints: No wind is needed. What are gas particles always doing?
Name the process.
solution: This is **diffusion**: the randomly moving smell particles spread out through the air from a high concentration at the pit to a lower concentration further away.

options.text: Oxygen
Ethanol
Mercury

feedback.b: Ethanol's boiling point (78 °C) is above 20 °C, so it is a liquid. It evaporates easily, which is why you can smell it, but it is not a gas at 20 °C.
feedback.c: Mercury melts at −39 °C and boils at 357 °C. 20 °C is between these, so it is a liquid metal.
feedback.d: 20 °C is below the melting point of sulfur (115 °C), so it is a solid.

hints: A substance is a gas when the temperature is above its boiling point.
solution: Oxygen's boiling point is −183 °C. Room temperature (20 °C) is far above that, so oxygen is a **gas**. Ethanol and mercury are liquids, and sulfur is a solid.

prompt: Yellow sulfur crystals form around geothermal vents near Rotorua. In the lab, some sulfur is heated to 200 °C, where it is a [[a]]. It is heated further to 500 °C, where it is a [[b]]. When this sulfur is cooled back down to 300 °C, it [[c]].
hints: Compare each temperature with 115 °C and 445 °C.
Cooling from 500 °C to 300 °C crosses one of these temperatures. Which change happens there?
solution: 200 °C is between the melting point (115 °C) and boiling point (445 °C), so sulfur is a **liquid**. 500 °C is above the boiling point, so it is a **gas**. Cooling to 300 °C takes it below 445 °C but not below 115 °C, so the gas **condenses** into a liquid. It doesn't freeze, because 300 °C is still above the melting point.

prompt: Which state of matter has **both** a fixed shape and a fixed volume?

options.text: Solid
Liquid
Gas
Liquid and gas

feedback.b: A liquid has a fixed volume, but it takes the shape of its container.
feedback.c: A gas has neither a fixed shape nor a fixed volume. It spreads out to fill its container.
feedback.d: Neither of these keeps its own shape: both take the shape of their container.

hints: Which state keeps its shape when you take it out of its container?
solution: A **solid** keeps its shape and its volume, because its particles are held in fixed positions.

prompt: What is the name for the temperature at which a solid turns into a liquid?
hints: It is named after the change of state from solid to liquid.
solution: It is the **melting point**. For example, the melting point of ice is 0 °C.

prompt: On a warm day, drops of water appear on the outside of a cold bottle of drink taken from the fridge. Where does this water come from?

options.text: Water vapour in the air cools on the cold bottle and condenses
The drink seeps out through tiny holes in the glass
The surface of the cold glass is melting
Nitrogen and oxygen in the air turn into liquid water

feedback.b: Glass does not let liquids through. Even a sealed, empty bottle from the fridge gets wet on the outside.
feedback.c: Glass is a solid that only melts at very high temperatures. A cold bottle is nowhere near that.
feedback.d: Nitrogen and oxygen cannot turn into water. They are different substances, and they only become liquid at around −200 °C.

hints: Air always contains some water as an invisible gas.
solution: The air contains invisible **water vapour**. When it touches the cold bottle, the water particles lose energy, slow down and come together as liquid droplets: **condensation**.

prompt: Match each physical property to its meaning.

right.text: Can be hammered or bent into shape without breaking
Can be stretched out into a thin wire
Breaks or shatters easily when hit
Does not let heat pass through easily
Lets an electric current flow through it

hints: A copper wire is ductile; a glass window is brittle.
solution: Malleable: can be hammered into shape. Ductile: can be drawn into wire. Brittle: shatters easily. Thermal insulator: doesn't let heat through easily (like the plastic handle of a pot). Electrical conductor: lets current flow (like copper).

prompt: On a cold, dry, sunny day high in the Southern Alps, some snow disappears without melting. The ice changes straight from a [[a]] into a [[b]]. This change of state is called [[c]].
hints: The snow never becomes liquid water.
solution: The ice goes straight from a **solid** to a **gas** (water vapour) without becoming a liquid. This is **sublimation**.

prompt: Overhead power lines sag lower on a hot summer day than on a cold winter day. Why?

options.text: The particles in the wire vibrate more and move slightly further apart, so the wire gets longer
The particles in the wire get bigger when they are hot, so the wire gets longer
Heat from the Sun adds extra particles to the wire, so the wire gets longer
The wire starts to melt in the heat, so it droops like a liquid

feedback.b: Particles do not change size when they are heated. The spaces between them get bigger.
feedback.c: No particles are added. The wire has the same mass in summer and winter.
feedback.d: Power lines are made of metals such as aluminium, which melts at about 660 °C. The wire is still a solid.

hints: What happens to the movement of particles in a solid when it is heated?
solution: When the wire is heated, its particles **vibrate more** and push slightly further apart. The wire **expands** (gets longer), so it sags more. The particles themselves stay the same size.

prompt: When water is boiling in a pot, large bubbles form and rise to the surface. What is inside these bubbles?

options.text: Water vapour (water as a gas)
Air
Hydrogen gas and oxygen gas
Nothing, they are empty space

feedback.b: The tiny bubbles that appear as water first warms up are dissolved air coming out. The big bubbles during boiling are water that has turned into a gas.
feedback.c: Boiling is a physical change. The water particles do not split apart; they just move far apart as a gas.
feedback.d: The bubbles push the water aside, so they must contain something: water particles in the gas state.

hints: Boiling is a change of state. What does liquid water turn into?
solution: During boiling, water turns into a gas all through the liquid, not just at the surface. The bubbles are pockets of **water vapour**, which rise and escape as steam.

prompt: On a clear night, dew forms on the grass. Put the steps in order.

items.text: After sunset, the grass loses heat and becomes cold
The air touching the cold grass cools down
Water vapour particles in this air lose energy and slow down
The water particles come together as droplets of liquid on the grass

hints: Dew is a kind of condensation. What has to get cold first?
solution: The grass cools after sunset, so the air touching it cools. The water vapour particles in that air lose energy and slow down, and they come together to form liquid **dew** droplets: condensation.

prompt: Nitrogen melts at −210 °C and boils at −196 °C. Over how many degrees Celsius is nitrogen a liquid?
hints: Nitrogen is a liquid between its melting point and its boiling point.
Count up from −210 to −196.
solution: Nitrogen is a liquid from −210 °C up to −196 °C. The difference is −196 − (−210) = **14 °C**.

prompt: Kiri stirs a spoonful of sugar into her hot tea and says, "The sugar has melted." What is the best reply?

options.text: It dissolved: the sugar particles spread out between the water particles
Yes, heat from the tea turned the solid sugar into liquid sugar
It reacted with the tea to make a new substance
It evaporated into the air, which is why you can no longer see it

feedback.b: Sugar only melts at about 186 °C, far hotter than a cup of tea. Sugar also disappears into cold water, which could not melt it.
feedback.c: Dissolving is a physical change. If the water evaporated, the sugar would be left behind.
feedback.d: The sugar is still in the tea. That is why the tea tastes sweet.

hints: Melting needs one substance on its own to be heated to its melting point. How many substances are involved here?
solution: The sugar has **dissolved**: its particles have separated and spread out between the water particles, too small to see. Melting is a solid turning into a liquid on its own when heated to its melting point (about 186 °C for sugar), which a cup of tea is nowhere near.

prompt: A balloon is blown up in a warm room and then put in a freezer. After an hour it has shrunk. When it is taken out and warms up, it swells back to its original size. Use the particle model to explain these observations.
modelAnswer: In the freezer the air particles in the balloon lose energy and move more slowly. They hit the inside of the balloon less often and less hard, so they push out on the rubber less and the balloon shrinks. When the balloon warms up again, the particles gain energy and move faster, hitting the inside of the balloon more often and harder, so it swells. The number of particles, and their size, stays the same the whole time.

rubric.criterion: In the cold, the air particles lose energy and move more slowly
Slower particles hit the inside of the balloon less often or less hard, so they push out less and the balloon shrinks
When warmed, the particles gain energy and move faster again, hitting the balloon more often or harder, so it swells (the number of particles stays the same)

hints: What keeps a balloon blown up? Think about the particles hitting the rubber.
Do any particles leave the balloon or change size?
solution: Cold: particles slow down and hit the walls less often and less hard, so the balloon shrinks. Warm: particles speed up and hit the walls more, so it swells. The particles themselves are unchanged.

prompt: Which statements about water **boiling** in a pot at sea level are correct? Select **all** that apply.

options.text: The water particles gain energy
The water particles move much further apart
The temperature stays at 100 °C while the water is boiling
The water particles get bigger
The water particles split into hydrogen and oxygen
The particles stop moving once they become a gas

hints: Boiling is a physical change.
Gas particles move fastest of all.
solution: When water boils, its particles **gain energy** and move **far apart** as a gas, and the temperature **stays at 100 °C** until it has all boiled. The particles do not change size or split up (it is still water), and gas particles move faster, not slower.

prompt: Water can be poured, but it is almost impossible to squash it into a smaller volume. Use the particle model to explain **both** of these facts.
modelAnswer: The particles in a liquid are not held in fixed positions. They can move and slide past each other, so the liquid flows and can be poured. But the particles are still very close together, touching each other with almost no empty space between them, so they cannot be pushed any closer and the liquid cannot be squashed.

rubric.criterion: Particles can move or slide past each other (not in fixed positions), so the liquid flows
Particles are close together with very little space between them, so they cannot be pushed closer (it cannot be compressed)

hints: Explain each fact separately: one is about movement, the other is about spacing.
solution: Pouring: liquid particles slide past each other. Not squashable: the particles are already touching, with almost no space between them.

prompt: A burn from steam at 100 °C is usually much worse than a burn from the same amount of boiling water at 100 °C. Explain why.
modelAnswer: When steam touches the skin, it condenses into liquid water. Condensing gives out a large amount of energy, the same energy the water took in when it boiled to become steam, and this energy goes into the skin. The water that forms is still at 100 °C, so it then gives out more heat as it cools down. Steam therefore transfers much more energy to the skin than boiling water, which only gives out heat as it cools.

rubric.criterion: Steam condenses into water when it touches the (cooler) skin
Condensing releases a large amount of energy (the energy taken in when it boiled) into the skin
The water formed is still at 100 °C and then gives out more heat as it cools, so steam transfers more energy in total than boiling water

hints: What happens to steam when it touches something cooler?
Turning water into steam takes a lot of energy. Where does that energy go when the steam turns back into water?
solution: Steam gives the skin two lots of energy: first the large amount released as it **condenses**, then the heat released as the hot water cools. Boiling water only gives the second.

prompt: Under a microscope, specks of smoke in a small glass cell of air look like bright dots. Each dot jiggles about randomly, even though the air is still. What is the best explanation?

options.text: Air particles, too small to see, are moving randomly and hitting each speck unevenly from all sides
The specks of smoke are tiny living things that are swimming about in the air
Warm air rising in the cell is carrying all of the specks of smoke upwards
The specks are vibrating in fixed positions, like the particles in a solid

feedback.b: Smoke is made of tiny bits of soot and ash, which are not alive. Specks of any non-living material jiggle like this.
feedback.c: Rising air would carry the specks smoothly in one direction. Here each speck jiggles in its own random way.
feedback.d: The specks wander around the cell rather than staying in one place, and they are floating in a gas, not held in a solid.

hints: Something invisible must be pushing the specks. What is the air made of, and what is it always doing?
solution: The air is made of particles that are far too small to see, moving fast and randomly. At any instant, more of them hit a speck on one side than the other, so it is knocked about in a random, jiggling path. This is evidence that the particles in a gas are constantly moving.

prompt: The particles in air move at hundreds of metres per second. Yet when someone opens a bottle of perfume on the far side of a still room, it takes a while before you can smell it. Why?

options.text: The perfume particles keep colliding with air particles, so they change direction constantly
Perfume particles move hundreds of times more slowly than air particles
The perfume must turn back into a liquid before it can travel across the room
Smell particles can only move when there is a wind to carry them

feedback.b: Perfume particles are heavier, so they move a little more slowly than air particles, but still very fast. The main reason is all the collisions.
feedback.c: The perfume spreads as a gas. It does not need to become a liquid.
feedback.d: Wind speeds it up, but diffusion happens even in completely still air, because the particles are always moving.

hints: A perfume particle is surrounded by a huge number of air particles. What happens when they meet?
solution: Each perfume particle moves very fast, but it **collides** with air particles billions of times a second, so its path is a zigzag that keeps changing direction. Overall it makes slow progress across the room. That is why diffusion in a gas is much slower than the speed of the particles.
